paras: The killing of Bob Crouch was the fatal shooting of a Black man on Main Street in Saluda, South Carolina, on the night of September 5, 1903. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of W. L. Rhoden, the sheriff of Saluda County, and Matt Berry, and the coroner arrested the sheriff. Papers treated the arrest of a sitting sheriff for murder as a rarity and followed his refusal to give up his office.

Just after dark, a pistol shot was heard near the corner of Main and Church streets, and Crouch was found in the street shot through the head. According to the News and Courier's Saluda correspondent, there had been no disturbance, and Crouch was standing alone in the street when he was shot. He died soon afterward as a crowd gathered, and an unloaded double-barreled shotgun lay beside him.

Coroner Jacob Gibson began an inquest that night, and several Black men were jailed as probable witnesses. On the first night no witness swore he knew who fired, although Pope Coleman, who had just left Crouch, said two white men had done it from the corner of a store. Recalled at the secret Sunday session, Coleman named the two as Sheriff Rhoden and Berry and said he had been afraid to speak for fear of being killed. Coleman and John Jeter swore that one of the two fired, they could not tell which, and Coleman said Berry had told Rhoden minutes earlier that he intended to kill a man, and Rhoden promised to help.

Other testimony was less certain: a drug store clerk saw pistol smoke and a man running up Church Street, while a boy said a man across the street raised his arm "like he was sighting" but could not tell whether he was white or Black. Berry, himself a witness, testified that the shot came from behind him and that he saw no one, and none of the white men nearby could say who fired. The all-white jury returned a verdict that Crouch died "at the hands of W. L. Rhoden and Matt Berry."

The coroner arrested the sheriff in a drug store, and Berry, who lived about eight miles out, came in and surrendered. The State's correspondent wrote that the few opinions voiced in town held the accused innocent, and that Rhoden had beaten Berry's brother for sheriff in 1902 by 15 votes.

Gibson wrote Governor D. C. Heyward that Rhoden refused to turn the office over to him or be locked up, discharged the jailer, the coroner's son, and was freed on habeas corpus while still acting as sheriff. Heyward, who had first said he had no official record, referred the question to Attorney General Gunter; a Columbia dispatch noted that state law barred the governor from removing a sheriff. Judge Townsend granted Rhoden and Berry bail of $1,000, and no report of an indictment or trial was found.

Coverage came from the white press of South Carolina and Georgia between September 10 and 25. The fullest accounts, Saluda specials to the News and Courier and The State reprinted in Newberry, Lancaster and Kingstree, gave the inquest testimony at length and called the victim "colored" and "the Crouch negro." A Columbia dispatch in the Savannah Morning News, which named the victim "Bob Church," called the arrest "a great sensation" and "the first time in many years" a South Carolina sheriff had been so charged, and was reprinted in Pickens and elsewhere.

Later stories turned from the victim to the office. Headlines such as "Sheriff a Murderer," "Reckless Sheriff Rhoden" and "A Sheriff Defies the Coroner" described a legal puzzle in which Crouch appeared only as "a negro." State-news columns in Anderson and Yorkville called it "a rare occurrence" and noted "local ignorance of the law." No coverage of the killing was found in the Black press.

The victim's name appeared as Bob Crouch in the Saluda specials, Bob Church in the Columbia wire, and Robert Granch or Robert Crane in the coroner's letter. The Columbia wire put the verdict and arrest on Monday evening, but both Saluda specials, written on September 7 and 8, place them on Sunday.

reader.title: Killing of Bob Crouch
bases: A coroner's jury charged the county sheriff, W. L. Rhoden, and a private man, Matt Berry, with shooting Crouch (A3, A5, A15); no report describes the shooting as an arrest or other official act, so the type rests on the sheriff's office alone.

Separate Saluda specials to the News and Courier (A3) and The State (A5), the Columbia wire (A1), and the coroner's own letter (A15, A16) agree on the shooting, the verdict and the arrests, though who fired rests on two witnesses' testimony.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury and Black witnesses
accounts.gist: Coleman and Jeter swore the shot came from Rhoden or Berry, standing by a brick store; Coleman said Berry had told Rhoden minutes earlier he meant to kill a man and Rhoden promised to help. The all-white jury named both men.

accounts.label: Berry's testimony
accounts.gist: Berry said the shot was fired behind him as he neared the drug store and that he saw no one where it came from.

accounts.label: Other witnesses
accounts.gist: A clerk saw pistol smoke and a man running up Church Street; a boy said he saw a man across the street raise his arm 'like he was sighting', but could not tell if he was white or Black; no white witness could say who fired.

accounts.label: Coroner's letter to the governor
accounts.gist: Gibson reported the Sept. 5 shooting, the verdict and arrests, and that the sheriff refused to surrender his office or be jailed, discharged the jailer and was freed on habeas corpus.

framing.detail: Saluda specials gave detailed inquest testimony under headlines like 'Sheriff Charged With Murder' and 'A Mysterious Murder ... Very Unusual Case', calling the victim 'colored' and 'the Crouch negro'.
The Columbia wire stressed the 'great sensation' of a sheriff's arrest and the 'first time in many years' such a charge was laid, and was reprinted across South Carolina.
Later headlines ('Sheriff a Murderer', 'Reckless Sheriff Rhoden', 'A Sheriff Defies the Coroner') turned to the office dispute, with the victim reduced to 'a negro'.

conflicts.note: Both local Saluda specials and the bail notice use Crouch; Church likely confuses the name with Church Street, and Granch/Crane are renderings of the coroner's letter.
The two Saluda specials, written on Sept. 7 and 8, both put the verdict on Sunday; the Columbia wire is later and secondhand.
The State's Monday special says 'This morning he came to Saluda and surrendered'; the News and Courier presumes a Sunday return.
